blocks.content: Lakshadweep's tiny land area and coral-atoll geography give it one of India's most specialised and narrowly-based economies, historically centred on coconut cultivation and fisheries, with tourism now rapidly emerging as a major growth sector.

Coconut cultivation has historically been the dominant land-based economic activity across the islands, given the coral-soil terrain's limited suitability for other crops; coconut and its by-products (copra, coir) have long been central to the islands' traditional economy and export trade with the Kerala mainland.

Fisheries — particularly tuna fishing — form the other traditional economic mainstay, with the pole-and-line tuna fishing method being a long-established, sustainable traditional practice distinctive to Lakshadweep's fishing communities, alongside processing and export of tuna and other fish products.

Because of the limited land area and coral-based soil, Lakshadweep has essentially no significant agriculture beyond coconut and minor subsistence crops, and no substantial industrial or manufacturing base, making the islands heavily dependent on imports from the Kerala mainland for most goods.

cells: Dominant traditional land-based crop; basis for copra and coir production
Traditional pole-and-line tuna fishing; major livelihood and export sector
Minimal, given coral-atoll soil constraints; heavy dependence on mainland imports for food and other goods
Negligible manufacturing base; economy dominated by primary-sector activity and, increasingly, tourism/services

blocks.content: Tourism has historically been tightly regulated in Lakshadweep, given the islands' small population, fragile coral-reef ecology, and the administration's longstanding policy of restricting visitor access (including special permit requirements for both Indian and foreign visitors) to protect the islands' environment and social fabric.

Tourism gained major national and international attention following Prime Minister Narendra Modi's visit to Lakshadweep in January 2024, during which he promoted the islands' pristine beaches and marine environment as a world-class tourism destination; this visit, and the accompanying social-media promotion, coincided with a significant, widely reported diplomatic row with the Maldives (after Maldivian officials made derogatory remarks about the visit and India's tourism promotion, prompting a wave of Indian public interest in Lakshadweep as an alternative destination and a temporary diplomatic downgrade in India-Maldives relations).

This 2024 episode produced a sharp, well-documented spike in domestic tourist interest and bookings for Lakshadweep, along with renewed government emphasis on expanding the islands' tourism infrastructure (Chapter 9) while attempting to balance this growth against the islands' fragile ecological carrying capacity and the 2021 regulatory controversies (Chapter 4) that had already heightened local sensitivity to rapid, externally-driven development.

★ EXAM POINT: PM Modi's January 2024 Lakshadweep visit and the resulting India-Maldives diplomatic row is one of the most important and frequently tested recent current-affairs episodes for this UT — remember it directly triggered a major, well-documented surge in Indian domestic tourism interest in the islands.

items: Coconut cultivation (copra, coir) and traditional pole-and-line tuna fishing are Lakshadweep's historic economic mainstays.
Negligible agriculture beyond coconut and minimal industry; heavy dependence on mainland Kerala for most goods.
Tourism has historically been tightly regulated (permit system) to protect fragile coral-reef ecology and social fabric.
PM Modi's January 2024 visit + the India-Maldives diplomatic row triggered a major surge in domestic tourism interest in Lakshadweep.
